title: Benchmark Recording Warm-Up and CPU Power-State Transients
pattern: A steady-state latency benchmark records samples from the first iteration, without untimed warm-up iterations and without fixing or verifying the CPU frequency governor, so measurements include cold caches, lazy initialization, C-state exits and dynamic frequency ramp-up.
why_bad: Early iterations measure power-state wake-up (~100 µs), instruction and data cache misses, page faults and first-time allocation rather than the operation. Dynamic frequency scaling can change clock speed several-fold mid-run, so short benchmarks vary run to run and comparisons between variants measure the governor, not the code.
detection: A measurement loop that records into its result histogram/statistics from index 0 with no preceding untimed warm-up phase, in a benchmark reporting steady-state numbers; or a benchmark harness or script with no step that sets or checks the CPU governor (`performance` mode) or validates cycle-counter/frequency consistency. Harnesses that warm up internally (e.g. Criterion) are not flagged.
counterexample: Benchmarks whose explicit subject is cold-start latency (process or serverless startup, first-request latency) or power-management behavior and energy efficiency.
source: Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics* (2021), Ch. 10, §10.3, p. 161; Ch. 22, p. 281; Ch. 29, §29.11, p. 370; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance* (2013), Ch. 12, §12.3, p. 593.
